— French aerospace company Safran has released a video offering a glimpse of some of the technologies being developed for the Dassault Rafale F5, the next major upgrade of the French multirole fighter.
The F5 standard will bring upgrades to the aircraft's propulsion, radar, electronic warfare and combat systems.
One of the main developments is Safran's M88 T-REX engine, designed to increase maximum afterburning thrust by approximately 20%, from 7.5 to 9 tonnes. The upgrades include a redesigned low-pressure compressor, a high-pressure turbine using new materials and advanced cooling systems, and an aerodynamically optimized exhaust nozzle. Despite these changes, the engine will retain the M88's modular architecture, dimensions and maintenance advantages.
The Rafale F5 will also receive Thales' RBE2-XG (eXtended Generation) AESA fire-control radar. Designed to fit within the existing RBE2 nose envelope, the new radar will replace the current RBE2-AA's gallium arsenide (GaAs) technology with gallium nitride (GaN). This will allow it to operate at higher power levels, extending its detection range and improving its ability to detect and identify targets with very low radar cross-sections. The radar will also have greater computing power to support artificial intelligence applications, along with improved resistance to electronic warfare and cyber threats.
The aircraft's electronic warfare and self-protection suite will be upgraded to the SPECTRA F5 standard, developed by Thales and MBDA. The new version will use an all-digital architecture, with improved threat detection and jamming capabilities to deal with increasingly sophisticated air-defence systems.
Another addition will be Thales' Inter-Vehicle Data Link (IVDL), a high-bandwidth communications system designed to provide secure, low-observable and jamming-resistant links between aircraft. It will allow Rafale F5 fighters to share information and coordinate their actions in heavily contested environments.
The Rafale F5 will also be designed to operate alongside a new stealth combat drone, being developed by Dassault Aviation, Thales and Safran. Building on experience gained from the nEUROn demonstrator, the unmanned aircraft will support the Rafale in air-to-air and air-to-ground missions. Its intended roles include penetrating hostile airspace and suppressing enemy air defences. The drone will incorporate low-observable features, advanced sensors, artificial intelligence and resilient communications.
The F5 will also be compatible with France's future ASN4G hypersonic nuclear air-launched missile, which is set to replace the ASMPA-R in the country's airborne nuclear deterrent.
The French Directorate General of Armaments (DGA) is targeting qualification of the Rafale F5 around 2033, ahead of its entry into service with the French Air and Space Force and the French Navy.

Iran's 358 loitering surface-to-air missile system was displayed atop a camouflage-covered mound at the "Miracle of Science and Faith" exhibition in Mashhad, Iran, which opened on November 25, 2026.
The 358 missile, placed on a display stand on the left side of the exhibit, is a subsonic, turbojet-powered loitering munition designed to patrol an area and engage low- to medium-altitude aerial targets, including drones and helicopters. It relies on passive optical and infrared sensors rather than active radar for target acquisition and engagement. The system has been used to shoot down several U.S. and Israeli unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
The display also includes the system's control and communications equipment: a ruggedized laptop/console unit on the central table and a tripod-mounted dish antenna on the right, identified in the accompanying caption as the uplink and downlink equipment.
